episodes.180125: Strong daytime heating and good moisture levels proved sufficient for scattered thunderstorm development up and down much of the High Plains on the afternoon and evening of the 23rd. In addition, a storm system emerging from the northern Rockies provided moderate to strong vertical wind shear over this same corridor, which promoted storm organization. Several of the thunderstorms gained strong mid-level rotation. These supercell thunderstorms generated very large hail and torrential downpours as they tracked eastward through the evening hours. One storm took aim at the south side of Lubbock (Lubbock County), producing golf ball to baseball size hail, and even larger in spots. The giant stones were widely spaced, but inflicted property damage where they impacted objects like cars and buildings.||High wind reports from the Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site are listed below:||67 mph at Paducah (Cottle County),|58 mph at Hackberry (Cottle County), and|58 mph at Childress (Childress County).||Maximum wind gusts from area ASOS stations are listed below:||59 mph at Childress Municipal Airport (Childress County).
episodes.180191: Thunderstorms moving offshore produced strong wind gusts along the Brevard and Treasure Coasts.
episodes.180323: A low pressure system across far southwestern South Dakota on the early evening of June 23rd shifted northeast through the night, and reached far northeastern South Dakota by 10am on the 24th. Thunderstorms developed in the vicinity of this system as well as along a stationary front, and quickly became strong to severe. While initially discrete, cells eventually merged into a squall line. As a result, both large hail and damaging wind gusts locally in excess of 80 mph resulted across central South Dakota.
episodes.180365: An intense, long-lived supercell initially developed near the town of Chugwater over the higher terrain of the central Laramie Range around 3:00 PM on 6/23, tracking to the east-southeast across southern Platte and Goshen Counties through approximately 7:00 PM. A small, terrain-driven area of low pressure and resultant cyclonic flow resulted in moisture pooling and backed, easterly near-surface flow near the track of the storm which resulted in a favorable environment for tornadoes. The cyclic supercell produced 5 separate confirmed tornadoes, most notably including an EF-2 tornado which developed near the town of Hawk Springs. A swath of large hail up to two inches in diameter also occurred with this storm. A separate storm over far northwestern Converse County also produced a brief tornado that afternoon. A second round of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted Platte and Goshen Counties later in the day.
episodes.180384: The most notable storm of the day was an intense, long-lived, cyclic tornadic supercell which significantly impacted Scotts Bluff and Morrill Counties during the early evening hours. This storm originated in the central Laramie Range of Wyoming approximately 50 miles to the west around 3 to 4 hours prior to reaching western Nebraska, producing several confirmed tornadoes along its path. Environmental conditions across Scotts Bluff County continued to support the potential for tornadoes, with abundant moisture pooling in the Platte River Valley and favorable east-to-southeast winds near the surface with a strong southwesterly jet stream aloft. The supercell produced 7 additional confirmed tornadoes (6 in Scotts Bluff County and 1 in Morrill County), most notably including an EF-2 tornado which tracked approximately 1-3 miles ENE of Gering between 7:38 PM and 7:45 PM MDT. A Tornado Emergency was in effect for Gering and Scottsbluff from 7:31 PM until 8:00 PM MDT, which was the first ever issuance of this product from the NWS in Cheyenne. Numerous instances of baseball to softball sized hail occurred across Scotts Bluff County including the city of Scottsbluff. A second intense supercell developed and tracked across Scotts Bluff County in the wake of the first tornadic storm, producing a second swath of very large (baseball sized) hail over the same area. In addition to this primary focus area for intense storms, other isolated storms also brought quarter sized hail, 60 MPH wind gusts to portions of the western Nebraska Panhandle.
episodes.180417: It was a stormy late-night/early Saturday morning across portions of South Central Nebraska, particularly within counties north of Interstate 80 where a few rounds of strong to (limited) severe thunderstorms rolled through from west-to-east mainly between 1:30-6:30 a.m. CDT. The majority of this activity produced sub-severe wind gusts and/or small hail, and in fact there was only one ground-truth report that officially breached severe criteria: a measured 68 MPH wind gust at the Ord airport ASOS...substantiated by an account of minor wind damage by the NWS Cooperative Observer in town. Although this was the only verified instance of severe weather locally, Severe Thunderstorm Warnings were in effect at some point for portions of all seven local counties north of Interstate 80. ||Turning to the meteorological background and event evolution, from a big picture perspective, northern portions of South Central Nebraska received only a glancing blow from a more concentrated swath of severe weather stretched across western and northern portions of the state. Initially, at least semi-discrete severe storms erupted over western Nebraska during the evening of the 23rd, with large-scale forcing focused along the southern fringes of a mid-upper level trough/closed low shifting from MT/WY into the Dakotas during the night. With time, the early activity grew upscale into the heart of a 40-50 knot southerly low-level jet axis (evident at 850 millibars) and a pair of convective lines merged into a more organized, north-south oriented linear mesoscale convective system (MCS) over central/north central Nebraska between 1-2 a.m. CDT...just prior to its southern reaches charging into the Valley County area and prompting the aforementioned severe wind gust. Between 3-4 a.m. CDT, as the initial complex shifted east of the Highway 281 corridor, a new cluster of strong storms flared up slightly to its west in its wake, with this later activity migrating through several local counties mainly along/north of I-80 before finally vacating South Central Nebraska for good between 5:30-6:30 a.m. CDT. Around the time of the severe-caliber gust at Ord airport, the mesoscale environment featured a decent combination of most-unstable CAPE 1500-2000 J/kg and deep-layer wind shear 30-40 knots.
episodes.180586: A tornadic thunderstorm developed over far southern Campbell County and tracked east-northeast into Weston County. The storm produced a large F-2 tornado that moved over the North Antelope Rochelle Coal Mine in far southeastern Campbell County, causing considerable damage and minor injuries at the mine. Large hail and wind gusts over 80 mph accompanied the storm.
episodes.180587: A line of thunderstorms developed and tracked across a good portion of Crook County, producing wind gusts over 60 mph.
episodes.180588: A strong thunderstorm produced hail to penny size in Saint Onge and heavy rain across the northern foothills area. Runoff from the heavy rain caused significant flooding in Spearfish and across other portions of northern Lawrence County. Asphalt buckled and gravel washed off numerous roads from the flooding and damaged buildings.
episodes.180590: A supercell thunderstorm developed over the northern Black Hills and tracked northeast across portions of Butte and northern Meade Counties. The storm produced large hail to at least golf ball size, along with wind gusts around 60 mph.
episodes.180593: A severe thunderstorm developed over eastern portions of Oglala Lakota County, producing large hail near Sharps Corner.
episodes.180594: A thunderstorm briefly became severe in the Rapid City area, producing hail mostly on the south and east sides of the city. Runoff from heavy rain caused flooding along Box Elder Creek.
episodes.180603: A thunderstorm briefly became severe west of Hermosa, producing hail around quarter size.
episodes.180604: A severe thunderstorm tracked across portions of southeastern Pennington County, producing wind gusts around 70 mph in the Scenic area.
episodes.180605: A thunderstorm briefly became severe over the southwestern Black Hills, producing a 60 mph wind gust west of Jewel Cave.
episodes.180606: A slow moving severe thunderstorm developed over northeastern Jackson County, producing large hail and strong wind gusts east of Belvidere.
episodes.180608: Large hail accompanied a severe thunderstorm that developed over central Jackson County.
episodes.180609: Strong to severe thunderstorms merged into a line across west central South Dakota during the late evening and tracked across south central South Dakota, producing wind gusts to 70 mph along with small hail.
episodes.180681: Scattered severe storms tracked across southeast Iowa during the mid-afternoon into early evening of June 24, producing large hail up to golf ball size in Van Buren County and tennis ball size hail near Ottumwa.||More organized clusters of severe storms tracked through Dubuque into far northwest IL during the evening and late night hours of June 24.  Another storm cluster moved through the Quad Cities, producing wind gusts to 70 mph at the Davenport ASOS and damage to trees and power poles.  An EF-0 tornado also tracked east along and north of I-80 near the Davenport Airport, causing sporadic minor tree and structure damage.  This storm impacted the Quad City Airshow grounds, while no visitors were present.
episodes.181132: A stationary thunderstorm producing heavy rain resulted in flash flooding near Roscoe and Red Lodge.
episodes.181175: The middle part of June was unusually stormy across the area. Numerous rounds of strong to severe storms impacted the region with multiple squall lines that produced severe winds as well as supercells that produced large hail and tornadoes.  Heavy rain also occurred over a multi-day period, which saturated the ground and led to some instances of flash flooding.  ||The synoptic pattern featured well above average 250 mb zonal wind anomalies, which were traceable back to an active subtropical jet stream.  Greater than average instability was also present, in part due to anomalously warm Gulf of Mexico SSTs.  This combination of above average shear from the active subtropical jet and above average instability from the warmer than average SSTs provided a synoptic environment favorable for severe weather as upper level shortwaves moving through the area.  This pattern persisted for many days, leading to an unusually large amount of severe weather.
episodes.181262: Runoff from heavy rain caused flooding across portions of southern Meade County. Several roads were flooded, with gravel washed off numerous roads.
episodes.181312: A front shifted south across Georgia which focused a moist and unsettled SW steering across NE FL and pushed storms offshore of the local Atlantic coast.
episodes.181332: By the evening of the 23rd, as an upper system moved out across the Central Plains, widespread thunderstorm development occurred across the Texas Panhandle into Rolling Plains. A mix of cellular and linear storms moved across western-north Texas during the late evening time frame, producing reports of severe wind gusts and sub-severe hail across the area.
episodes.181339: Severe thunderstorms developed across the Big Country and Concho Valley during the late afternoon and evening hours. The storms mainly produced damaging winds and a few reports of large hail.
episodes.181559: An unstable airmass with a minor weather disturbance resulted in afternoon showers and thunderstorms, with locally severe weather occurring. Isolated locations also experienced flooding, such as portions of Jefferson County where Milligan Canyon Road was washed out in several locations.
episodes.181672: A decaying thunderstorm complex moved across the region on the morning of June 24 and produced a wake low that caused gusty non-thunderstorm winds. Flying Cloud airport in the Twin Cities gusted to 62 mph.||Later that afternoon a few storms developed and produced sub-severe hail and a funnel cloud. ||A third round of storms developed during the evening and produced one report of severe hail.
episodes.181725: A low pressure system slowly dropping SE form the eastern Dakotas and SW Minnesota dragged a cold front across the state during the evening and overnight hours of the 24th of June. Within the warm sector, MUCAPE values peaked in excess of 3000 J/kg during peak heating and scaled back a bit overnight but remained around or in excess of 2000 J/kg. Effective shear values were supportive for organized convection, residing in the 35 to around 50 kt range. Morning and lingering convective activity likely played a role in initiating some storms with remnant outflow boundaries around. As a result, a number of isolated or clustered organized storms were seen during the evening and overnight hours and produced a number of reports of large hail and damaging winds. The largest hail reported was 3 inches in both Palo Alto and Black Hawk counties. A couple of funnel clouds were reported as well.
episodes.181740: A cluster of storms impacted parts of northeast Iowa during the afternoon and into the evening of June 24th. Besides heavy rain, with 1.67 inches recorded in New Hampton (Chickasaw County) and 2.10 inches recorded near Elkport (Clayton County), damaging winds and hail also affected the area. Reports included tree damage in Oelwein (Fayette County) and 1 inch hail near Westgate (Fayette County).
episodes.181863: There were 2 rounds of severe weather in northeast Nebraska. A supercell developed in the early evening causing damage in Cedar County and a personal weather station observed a 73 mph wind gust.  A 2nd round of storms developed in western Nebraska and progressed across the state. It moved into eastern Nebraska in the morning hours of the 24th and resulted it a couple severe criteria wind reports.
episodes.181874: A long-lived supercell tracked across Knox and Cedar counties and resulted in a few severe hail reports the largest of which as 1.25 inches.
episodes.181875: A severe storm developed in Pottawattamie County and produced 1-inch hail.
episodes.182030: Severe thunderstorms produced large hail across parts of Logan, Morgan and Sedgwick counties.  The hail ranged from half dollar to tennis ball size.
episodes.182084: Numerous hail and wind reports were observed across far southwestern Kansas. A tornado was also reported.
episodes.182085: Despite the presence of a high pressure ridge over the Southern Plains, a plume of Gulf moisture extending north into the region allowed some afternoon convection to overcome subsidence provided by the ridge. Multiple thunderstorms developed, some of which produced large hail and damaging winds.
episodes.182239: On the evening of June 23rd, severe to destructive thunderstorms developed within East-Central Colorado just south of Interstate 70 and progressed north-northeast through the region. These thunderstorms produced destructive hail up to baseballs in size.
episodes.182242: On the evening of June 23rd, isolated thunderstorms developed along the Colorado and Kansas border and progressed eastward across Northwestern Kansas. A few of these thunderstorms became severe and produced hail up to quarters in size along with sub-severe wind gusts up to 57 mph.
episodes.182312: Surface low pressure system tracked across the North Dakota/South Dakota border creating an environment supporting the threat for low top supercells in Southeastern North Dakota into adjacent West Central Minnesota. Several low-top supercells developed and tracked along portions of the Minnesota Red River Valley. Portions of Norman, Polk, Becker, and Mahnomen counties saw multiple tornadoes. Large hail and damaging winds accompanied some of these storms, and flash flooding in some locations as well.
episodes.182365: Upper level disturbances moved across the region on the periphery of a ridge aloft. This produced multiple days of stormy weather with some storms becoming severe.
episodes.182385: A stationary front draped across the area helped to spark an expansive severe weather outbreak across western and north central Nebraska. Thunderstorm wind gusts up to 82 MPH, hail up to softball size, along with flash flooding was reported.
episodes.182413: A stubborn stalled frontal boundary that had been in place for multiple days continued to be the focal point for thunderstorm development. Even though it was night time, thunderstorms over the marine areas were able to maintain strong/severe intensity due to warmer surface water temperatures. This is quite common during the summertime along the Gulf Coast, especially with a frontal boundary in place. A storm near the Mouth of the Mississippi River was able to reach severe limits.
episodes.182434: Linear storms developed near a frontal boundary, moving across southeast South Dakota and into northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota early on June 24. Within an environment of shear, a strong low-level jet, and strong DCAPE, some storms produced severe-level winds.
episodes.182443: Linear storms developed near a frontal boundary, moving across southeast South Dakota and into northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota early on June 24. Within an environment of shear, a strong low-level jet, and strong DCAPE, some storms produced severe-level winds.
episodes.182444: Linear storms developed near a frontal boundary, moving across southeast South Dakota and into northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota early on June 24. Within an environment of shear, a strong low-level jet, and strong DCAPE, some storms produced severe-level winds.
episodes.182452: A strong upper-level wave across northeastern South Dakota ignited isolated afternoon thunderstorms near a cold front across south central South Dakota. Storms thrived and became briefly supercellular in a highly sheared and unstable environment while tracking eastward south of South Dakota Highway 46 into the early evening.  After a brief decrease in intensity entering Iowa, storms strengthened once again mid to late evening moving east of Cherokee generally along and south of Iowa Highway 3 with a variety of severe weather types.
episodes.182541: Various discrete and scattered thunderstorms impacted portions the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles each evening and overnight on the 21st through the 23rd. Several of these storms produced large hail over and inch in diameter with some as large as 2.75. Severe wind gusts were also hazard with a gust upwards of 66 mph measured by ground equipment. A supercell even dropped a tornado in Hemphill County.
episodes.182630: Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms developed across parts of East Texas on the afternoon of June 23rd, aided by forcing for ascent from weak warm air advection and downstream of a significant but weakening cluster of storms shifting southeast from the middle Red River Valley. This was also focused along the eastern periphery of a plume of warm, capping elevated mixed-layer air, which supported instability up to 4000 J/kg for boundary layer moisture characterized by mid 70s dew points. Under 25-30 knots of northwesterly flow around 500 millibars, deep-layer shear was marginally supportive for the evolution of supercells, and an upscale growing organized cluster as convective inhibition weakened in the peak late afternoon heating. The environment was at least conditionally supportive of large hail and increasing damaging winds, which ultimately occurred across parts of Rusk County and adjacent Panola County with multiple local storm reports.
episodes.182832: Exceptionally severe weather continues over southern Colorado with the continued deluge of moist air coming from the Pacific and remnant moisture from previous moisture from widespread heavy rainfall. The most notable weather feature was an EF3 tornado that hit a farm located in Prowers County. This was only the 3rd EF3 tornado recorded since NWS modernization in 1995.
episodes.183031: Surface low-pressure system tracked across the North Dakota/South Dakota border creating an environment supporting the threat for low-top supercells in Southeastern North Dakota.

A large cone tornado developed just east of US-85 south of Hawk Springs, before quickly becoming rain-wrapped. The tornado snapped cottonwood trees, with a tree branch impaling a stucco house. It also damaged outbuildings and snapped power poles. An injury occurred when the tornado flipped an 18-wheeler and injured the driver. The same tornado tracked to the southeast and damaged another outbuilding and a barn 3 miles southeast of Hawk Springs. The tornado was officially rated an EF-2. In addition to the tornado damage, straight-line winds from the Rear Flank Downdraft (RFD) damaged several hardwood trees. This is consistent with 100 MPH winds.

There was also a second damaging tornado, rated EF-1, that occurred this day on June 23, 2023. This tornado drifted across mostly open rural land across far southern Baca County east of Campo, Colorado for most of its lifespan. At a point during the middle of the tornadoes life, it impacted an abandoned farm stead, damaging two structures on the property. After hitting this property, it continued to track eastward across County Road 43, where it knocked down wooden power poles. Also at this time, the tornado passed a couple hundred yards to the north of an occupied family farm, but no damage was reported at this location. After crossing County Road 43, the tornado drifted back into open countryside and began deviating to the NNE, where it eventually dissipated near County Road 45.

Someone on twitter sent us a video of a tornado on the ground 6W of Callaway. The tornado occurred in an open field, which mitigated any damage it would have caused. Therefore, EF-U rating assigned with an estimated path length and width.

Spotter sent us a photo of a tornado on the ground via Twitter. It occurred in open fields, which mitigated any damage. Therefore, the rating of EF-U has been assigned with estimated path width and length.
A trained spotter reported that the funnel reached about halfway to the ground southwest of Janesville, MN.

Spotter called with reports of a tornado with intermittent touchdown near Waubun, MN. It occurred in open fields, which mitigated any damage. Therefore, the rating of EF-U has been assigned with an estimated path width and length.
Trained spotter reported hail, with largest stones being quarter sized.
Brief spin up was reported in an open field which mitigated any damage. Therefore, the rating of EF-U has been assigned with estimated path width and length.
Public reported a brief funnel cloud north of Boone. Image viewed on social media.
Large hail up to half dollar size was shown in social media picture.

Norman county Emergency Manager confirmed tornado touchdown east of Shelly, heading N-NW. This tornado lifted across the county line into Polk county. It occurred in open fields, which mitigated any damage. Therefore, the rating of EF-U has been assigned with an estimated path width and length.

Tornado confirmed to go through a tree grove near Lockhart and cause damage. Damage to softwood trees was found with no other damage discerned as it tracked northwest into open fields thus the tornado was given an EF-0 rating.

This is a tornado that continued into Polk county from Norman Co. It moved into an open fields, which mitigated any damage and quickly diminished. Therefore, the rating of EF-U has been assigned with an estimated path width and length.

This tornado touched down south of Mahnomen at 4:15 PM. The highest damage it caused was rated as an EF-2. Among the damage it caused as it continued across its 6 mile path was trees snapped and uprooted (both hard and soft wood), metal garage slid off its foundation and collapsed, crop damage, Quonset caved in on one side, roofing blown off homes, broken power line poles, and lifting fuel tankers full of 250 gallons of fuel and throwing them at a barn. Damage dollar amounts are estimated.
Hail up to walnut size was accompanied by heavy rainfall.
Crop damage is an estimate from insured losses. Information provided by the United States Department of Agriculture.
